positions/pro-choice-christian/oneLine: While abortion is a serious moral decision, the pregnant woman, as a moral agent before God, should be able to make it in conscience, and the law should not criminalise it; the church’s role is pastoral support rather than coercion.
positions/pro-choice-christian/coreClaim: Scripture does not explicitly address abortion, and the moral status of the early embryo is contested.
Women are full moral agents whose conscience and circumstances must be respected.
Criminalising abortion harms women, especially the poor, without reducing it effectively.
Christians should work to reduce the need for abortion through social justice, healthcare and support.
positions/pro-choice-christian/origin: Emerged in mainline Protestant and Jewish bodies in the 1960s–70s, which supported legal reform before Roe v. Wade (1973); the Religious Coalition for Abortion Rights (1973, now Religious Coalition for Reproductive Choice) and feminist ethicists such as Beverly Harrison (1983) articulated it; Catholics for Choice (1973) dissent from Catholic teaching.
positions/pro-choice-christian/strongest: There is genuine moral and scientific debate about when personhood begins, on which a pluralist state should not impose one religious view.
Historical evidence shows criminalisation leads to dangerous illegal abortions.
Jesus’ compassion toward women in difficult situations favours support over judgement.
Most Christian traditions hold that it contradicts the unanimous early church teaching against abortion (Didache; Athenagoras; Basil).
Critics argue that if the unborn is a human being, a woman’s autonomy cannot override its right to life.
Several denominations that adopted pro-choice positions have since qualified them (e.g. Southern Baptists reversed in 1980).
positions/pro-choice-christian/responses: Advocates reply that respecting conscience does not mean approving every abortion, and that ancient condemnations also concerned infanticide and sexual immorality.
They argue that reducing abortion is better achieved through social support than criminal law.
positions/pro-choice-christian/consequen: Mainline Protestant support for legal abortion in the US and Europe.
Polarisation between denominations in American politics.
positions/desert-spirituality/name: Desert spirituality (the Desert Fathers and Mothers)
positions/desert-spirituality/oneLine: Leave the world’s distractions to fight the passions in solitude, through prayer, fasting, manual work and obedience to an elder, so that the heart may be purified and come to love God and neighbour.
positions/desert-spirituality/coreClaims: Renunciation (Matthew 19:21) frees the heart for God.
The monk battles demons and the "thoughts" (logismoi) through watchfulness and prayer.
An elder (abba or amma) gives a "word" to guide each disciple.
Humility, hospitality and not judging others are the fruit of true asceticism.
positions/desert-spirituality/keyTexts/4: Apophthegmata Patrum (Sayings of the Desert Fathers)
positions/desert-spirituality/origin: Emerged in Egypt from around 270, when Antony withdrew to the desert, and with Pachomius’ communal monasteries (c.320); flourished at Nitria, Kellia and Scetis and in Palestine and Syria; written down in the Sayings of the Desert Fathers and by Evagrius and Cassian.
positions/desert-spirituality/strongestA: It follows Jesus’ call to leave all and his own forty days in the desert.
Its psychological insight into temptation and the passions remains remarkable.
It produced a whole culture of spiritual direction, humility and charity.
positions/desert-spirituality/strongestO: Reformers judged monastic vows a human work with no command of God, and withdrawal a flight from vocation in the world.
Some ascetic practices (extreme fasting, pillar-sitting) seem to despise the body God created.
Its two-tier picture of Christians (monks and the rest) is criticised as unbiblical.
positions/desert-spirituality/responses/: The desert tradition itself warned against excessive asceticism and pride, insisting on discretion (diakrisis).
Orthodox and Catholic writers stress that monastic life is a particular calling, not a higher grade of salvation.
positions/desert-spirituality/consequenc: Spread of monasticism East and West.
Desert sayings inspired modern spirituality and the eight-thoughts tradition (seven deadly sins).
positions/hesychasm-jesus-prayer/oneLine: In stillness (hesychia), with the mind gathered into the heart, the Christian repeats the name of Jesus, "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me", and by grace may come to see the uncreated light of God.
positions/hesychasm-jesus-prayer/coreCla: Unceasing prayer is possible through constant invocation of the name of Jesus.
Watchfulness (nepsis) guards the heart against thoughts.
The body participates in prayer (breathing, posture), since the whole person is to be deified.
The light seen by saints is the uncreated energy of God, the light of Tabor (Palamas).
positions/hesychasm-jesus-prayer/origin: Rooted in the desert "monologic" prayer and Diadochus of Photice (5th c.), developed on Sinai (John Climacus) and by Symeon the New Theologian (c.1000), and defended on Athos by Gregory Palamas, whose teaching councils at Constantinople upheld in 1341 and 1351.
positions/hesychasm-jesus-prayer/stronge: It answers Paul’s call to pray without ceasing in a simple, portable form.
It holds together doctrine (the incarnate name, deification) and experience.
Its witness to holiness in saints like Seraphim of Sarov is widely admired.
Barlaam of Calabria mocked psychosomatic techniques as "navel-gazing" and denied that the divine light could be uncreated.
Western critics question the essence-energies distinction behind it.
Protestant critics fear repetitive formulas (Matthew 6:7) and technique.
positions/hesychasm-jesus-prayer/respons: Hesychasts reply that the prayer is not a technique but humble supplication, practised under guidance, and that "vain repetition" refers to heathen babbling, not the tax collector’s plea.
positions/lectio-divina/oneLine: Scripture is read slowly, aloud and prayerfully, ruminated in the heart, answered in prayer and rested in before God: reading becomes an encounter rather than study.
positions/lectio-divina/coreClaims/0: God speaks personally through the Scriptures read in faith.
positions/lectio-divina/coreClaims/1: The text is "chewed" and repeated (ruminatio) until it shapes the heart.
positions/lectio-divina/coreClaims/2: Four movements: lectio, meditatio, oratio, contemplatio (Guigo II).
positions/lectio-divina/coreClaims/3: Reading is rooted in the liturgy and community.
positions/lectio-divina/origin: Practised by Origen and the Fathers, prescribed in the Rule of Benedict (c.530) and formulated by Guigo II the Carthusian (12th c.); revived after Vatican II (Dei Verbum 25) and adopted by many Protestants.
positions/lectio-divina/strongestArgumen: It keeps prayer anchored in Scripture.
It is simple and accessible to all.
positions/lectio-divina/strongestObjecti: Some Protestants worry that seeking a personal word can detach texts from their context and meaning.
Critics of its fourth step see a drift into wordless mysticism.
positions/lectio-divina/responses/0: Practitioners insist that meditation follows careful reading and that contemplation is God’s gift, not a technique.
positions/benedictine-spirituality/oneLi: A balanced common life of liturgical prayer, sacred reading and manual work under a rule and an abbot, marked by humility, obedience, stability and hospitality, seeks God in ordinary days.
positions/benedictine-spirituality/coreC: The Divine Office (Opus Dei) is the centre of the day; nothing is to be preferred to it.
Work and prayer are both service of God.
Humility is a ladder of twelve steps; obedience and listening shape the self.
positions/benedictine-spirituality/origi: Based on Benedict of Nursia’s Rule (c.530, Monte Cassino), spread by Gregory the Great and Carolingian reform, renewed at Cluny (910) and by the Cistercians (1098); influential beyond monasteries through Anglican and ecumenical oblates.
positions/benedictine-spirituality/stron: Its moderation and realism made it durable for 1,500 years.
It integrates body, community and prayer.
Monasteries preserved learning and served the poor.
Reformers criticised vows and the merit attached to monastic life.
Wealthy monasteries drifted from their ideals, prompting repeated reforms.
positions/benedictine-spirituality/respo: Benedictines answer that the Rule is a "little rule for beginners" and that reform is built into its history.
positions/benedictine-spirituality/conse: Western monastic civilisation; the Daily Office in Anglican and Lutheran churches.
positions/franciscan-spirituality/oneLin: Follow the poor and crucified Christ literally: embrace poverty, minority and joy, see all creatures as brothers and sisters, and love God affectively through meditation on the humanity and passion of Jesus.
positions/franciscan-spirituality/coreCl: Gospel poverty imitates the Christ who became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9).
Creation is a family praising God (Canticle of the Creatures).
Devotion focuses on the crib and the cross.
positions/franciscan-spirituality/keyTex: Bonaventure, The Soul’s Journey into God
positions/franciscan-spirituality/origin: Began with Francis of Assisi’s conversion and the approval of his brotherhood (1209), the Poor Clares (1212) and the Third Order; his stigmata at La Verna (1224) became an icon of union with the crucified; Bonaventure gave it theological form.
positions/franciscan-spirituality/strong: It recovers the Gospel’s literal call to poverty and joy.
It inspired care for the poor, peace-making and love of creation.
Its devotion made Christ’s humanity vivid for lay people (the Christmas crib, the Stations of the Cross).
Disputes over absolute poverty split the order (Spirituals versus Conventuals) and were condemned by John XXII in 1323.
Protestants questioned vows and stigmata; modern critics see some devotion as sentimental.
positions/franciscan-spirituality/respon: Franciscans point to continual reform (Observants, Capuchins) as fidelity to Francis.
positions/franciscan-spirituality/conseq: Mendicant orders; Stations of the Cross and crib devotion.
positions/rhineland-mysticism/oneLine: Through detachment (Gelassenheit) the soul lets go of all images and self-will, and in its innermost ground God gives birth to the Word; union with God lies beyond concepts.
positions/rhineland-mysticism/coreClaims: God is beyond every name and image (apophatic theology).
Detachment empties the soul so that God may fill it.
The birth of the Son takes place in the ground of the soul.
True mysticism shows itself in ordinary works done without a "why".
positions/rhineland-mysticism/origin: Developed among German Dominicans preaching to Beguines and nuns: Meister Eckhart (d. c.1328), Johannes Tauler (d.1361) and Henry Suso (d.1366), with Jan van Ruusbroec in Flanders and the anonymous Theologia Germanica, which Luther published in 1516-18.
positions/rhineland-mysticism/strongestA: It expresses God’s transcendence and the depth of union with God.
It influenced Luther (Tauler, Theologia Germanica) as well as Catholic mystics.
Its emphasis on detachment and humility is practical, not merely speculative.
positions/rhineland-mysticism/strongestO: John XXII condemned 28 of Eckhart’s propositions (1329) as heretical or suspect, e.g. on the soul’s uncreated element.
Critics see pantheist tendencies and indifference to sacraments and works.
Word-centred Protestants judge its wordless union as bypassing Christ and Scripture.
positions/rhineland-mysticism/responses/: Defenders argue Eckhart’s paradoxes were preaching rhetoric within orthodox theology; Tauler and Suso themselves corrected misreadings.
positions/rhineland-mysticism/consequenc: Shaped German devotion, Luther’s early theology and later Pietism.
